title: Word Search — DFS backtracking on grid.
shortTitle: Word Search — depth-first search with backtracking on a grid

s1_definition.profdef: Word Search asks whether a given word can be formed in a grid of characters by moving to horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, where each cell may be used at most once per path. The standard solution is depth-first search with backtracking: from each starting cell you explore a path matching the word character by character, temporarily marking visited cells, and you undo the mark when a branch fails so the cell becomes available for other paths.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture the National Bank of India's fraud team looking at a grid of letters pulled from scrambled transaction memos. They want to know if a suspicious codeword like "FRAUD" is hidden as a connected trail through adjacent cells. An investigator starts on an F, tries a neighbor that is R, then A, and so on; if a trail dead-ends, they step back and erase their footprints so another trail can reuse those cells.
s1_definition.oneliner: Try every starting cell, walk adjacent cells matching the word, mark cells as you enter and unmark as you leave, so backtracking frees them for other paths.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Word Search asks whether a given word can be formed in a grid of characters by moving to horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, where each cell may be used at most once per path. The standard solution is depth-first search with backtracking: from each starting cell you explore a path matching the word character by character, temporarily marking visited cells, and you undo the mark when a branch fails so the cell becomes available for other paths.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture the National Bank of India's fraud team looking at a grid of letters pulled from scrambled transaction memos. They want to know if a suspicious codeword like "FRAUD" is hidden as a connected trail through adjacent cells. An investigator starts on an F, tries a neighbor that is R, then A, and so on; if a trail dead-ends, they step back and erase their footprints so another trail can reuse those cells.

**One line to remember:** Try every starting cell, walk adjacent cells matching the word, mark cells as you enter and unmark as you leave, so backtracking frees them for other paths.

sections.s2_technical:
The grid is a two-dimensional character array. The word is a string. We must find a connected path, moving up, down, left, or right, whose characters spell the word, with no cell reused within that single path.

The outer loop tries every cell as a possible starting point. From a start, we call a recursive depth-first search that takes the current row, column, and the index into the word we are trying to match. The base success case is when the index equals the word length, meaning we matched every character. The failure cases are going out of bounds, landing on a cell that does not match the current character, or landing on a cell already used in this path.

To mark a cell as used, a common trick is to temporarily replace its character with a sentinel such as the hash symbol, then restore it after exploring. This avoids allocating a separate visited matrix. We recurse into the four neighbors for the next word index. If any neighbor returns true, we propagate true. After exploring all neighbors, we restore the original character, which is the backtracking step.

The time complexity is roughly O(m times n times 4 to the power L) in the worst case, where L is the word length, because from each cell we branch into up to four directions for each character. In practice the matching constraint prunes most branches quickly.

A senior nuance: restoring the character on the way out is essential; if you forget, cells stay permanently marked and valid words get rejected. Another nuance is to short-circuit as soon as one path succeeds rather than exploring all paths.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's anti-fraud unit receives grids of characters extracted from obfuscated wire-transfer memos. Fraud rings hide codewords such as a mule account tag by spreading letters across adjacent cells. The unit needs to confirm whether a specific codeword can be traced as a connected path.

This is exactly how Word Search works. We look for the word as a connected trail of adjacent matching cells.

Problem 2 — A letter cell must not be counted twice within the same trail, otherwise a single stray letter could falsely "complete" a word and raise a false alarm that freezes an innocent customer's account.

This is exactly why we mark a cell on entry and unmark it on exit, so within one path each cell is used at most once, but the cell is still free for other candidate paths.

The code will have an `Account` class for flavor, a `FraudWordSearch` class with an `exists` method running DFS plus backtracking, and a runnable demo that searches a grid for both a present and an absent codeword with logging.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a 3-by-4 character grid and the codeword "FRAUD".

Step 1: The outer loop reaches cell [0][0] which holds F, matching index 0 of "FRAUD". We mark it with a sentinel and recurse for index 1 expecting R.

Step 2: The neighbor [0][1] holds R, matching index 1. We mark and recurse for index 2 expecting A.

Step 3: The neighbor [0][2] holds A, matching index 2. We recurse for index 3 expecting U. The down neighbor [1][2] holds U, matching index 3. We recurse for index 4 expecting D. The down neighbor [2][2] holds D, matching index 4.

Step 4: We recurse for index 5, which equals the word length, so the base case returns true. The true result propagates back up the chain. As each frame returns, it restores its cell, but since we found the word the method returns true overall.

Step 5: For the absent word "SAFE", no starting cell holds S, so every DFS returns false and the method returns false.

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 12:40:00 INFO    Priya Sharma scan: codeword 'FRAUD' present? true
2026-10-27 12:40:00 INFO    codeword 'SAFE' present? false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  exists(board, "FRAUD")
    │
    ▼
  outer loop tries each start cell
    │ finds F at [0][0]
    ▼
  DFS index 0: F [0][0] mark '#'
    │
    ├─→ R [0][1] mark '#'
    │     └─→ A [0][2] mark '#'
    │           └─→ U [1][2] mark '#'
    │                 └─→ D [2][2] mark '#'
    │                       └─→ index==len → TRUE
    ▼
  backtrack restores all cells; result propagated = TRUE

  (for "SAFE": no S start cell → FALSE)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Word Search asks whether a given word can be formed in a grid of characters by moving between horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, where each cell can be used at most once within a single path. The natural solution is depth-first search combined with backtracking, which means I explore one candidate trail as deeply as possible, and whenever a trail fails I step back and undo my changes so the cells become available for other trails.

Concretely, I try every cell in the grid as a possible starting point, and from each start I run a recursive search that carries the current row, the current column, and the index of the character in the word I am trying to match. The search succeeds when the index reaches the length of the word, and it fails when I go out of bounds, when the cell does not match the expected character, or when the cell is already part of the current path.

The key detail is how I mark a cell as used and then release it. A clean trick is to temporarily overwrite the cell with a sentinel character so the mismatch check naturally rejects it during this path, and then to restore the original character after exploring all four directions. That restoration is the backtracking step, and forgetting it is the classic bug, because cells would stay permanently marked and legitimate words would be wrongly rejected. I also short-circuit as soon as any direction returns success.

In my project at National Bank of India, the anti-fraud unit received grids of characters pulled from obfuscated wire-transfer memos, and fraud rings hid codewords as connected trails across adjacent cells. The depth-first search with backtracking let us confirm whether a specific codeword was present without ever double-counting a single letter inside one trail, which mattered because a false positive could wrongly freeze an innocent customer's account.
